audio_caption: The audio clip begins with a single female speaker introducing that she will discuss "the right side of the heart," including "internal features." She mentions that the view is "posterior" and that a "wrinkle or sulcus" helps separate "the right ventricle versus the left ventricle." She will be "open[ing] up this right side of the heart." Next, she talks about the base of the heart where she will find the "superior and inferior vena cava." She states that putting a probe through the superior will exit out the inferior vena cava. The speaker specifies the ends of the superior and inferior vena cava feed into the right side of the heart and deposit blood into the right atrium.

A woman begins by stating she is going to cut along a probe in a calm, instructional tone. She explains she is opening the right atrium to see inside. After a pause, she describes how the chamber appears as a small entrance to the heart. Next, she describes how she will cut down along the edge of a wrinkle toward the apex to open the right ventricle. She then says she will turn the heart upside down before continuing to cut into the right side of the heart. She concludes by reminding the audience she cannot cut all the way to the apex because it is part of the left ventricle.

The audio features a single female speaker, who starts by saying "All right, so now" and then describes how she is going to flip a heart upright and open up the right side of it. She says again that "here... is the right atrium we looked at earlier" and continues to describe features of the right ventricle, noting the thickness of the wall. The speaker compares the thickness of the wall of the ventricle to that of the atrium, stating that the atrium's wall is much narrower.

The audio clip appears to be a lecture, delivered in an informative tone by a single female speaker, who describes the structure and function of the heart's tricuspid valve, its associated chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, emphasizing how the valve prevents backflow and the chordae tendineae prevent inversion.

The audio clip features a single, female speaker in an informative tone. She describes the layers of the ventricle wall, identifying "major layers" and naming the "epicardium," "myocardium," and "endocardium."

The audio clip begins with a female speaker providing anatomical details, mentioning opening up the right side to reveal a feature coming across the right side of the heart. Describing it as something that "looks like a papillary muscle," she names it the "moderator band," explaining that it "allows for electrical conduction." Her tone is informative and clear.

The audio clip features one female speaker in an instructional tone, describing how to open up the right side of a heart. She identifies the posterior view, right atrium, right ventricle, and a major vessel. Then, she flips the heart to show the anterior view, calling attention to the pulmonary trunk on the right side. She explains placing a probe into the pulmonary trunk, then flipping it back over to show the connection to the right ventricle. Finally, she reiterates the role of the pulmonary trunk, which is to carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
